steps.line: More than 2,300 years ago, a merchant named Zeno sailed from Phoenicia with a cargo of precious purple dye.
Near Athens, the ship was wrecked. The cargo, the fortune, all of it went into the sea.
Zeno made it ashore with almost nothing. He was about thirty, in a city where he knew no one.

steps.q: Broke and alone in a strange city, where does Zeno end up?
o: At the harbor, looking for work
At a temple, praying for his cargo
steps.why: A bookshop, of all places. Diogenes Laertius, who tells the story, says he sat down by a bookseller in Athens.

steps.line: He wandered into a bookshop and sat down. The bookseller was reading aloud from a book about Socrates.
Zeno was hooked. Socrates questioned everything, owned almost nothing, and wasn’t afraid. Zeno had lost everything, and found his life’s work.

steps.q: Zeno asked the bookseller where men like Socrates could be found. What happened?
o: The bookseller became his first teacher
Just then a philosopher walked by: “Follow him”
He was told such men were all long dead
steps.why: Diogenes Laertius says the Cynic Crates happened to pass, and the bookseller pointed: follow that man. Zeno did, and studied for years before he taught.

steps.line: Years later, the story goes, Zeno looked back and said: “I made a good voyage when I was shipwrecked.”

steps.q: Zeno taught in the Painted Porch on the Athens marketplace. What did that give his followers?
o: Their dress: robes painted like the walls
Their rule: only teach out of doors
Their name: Stoics, from stoa, porch
steps.why: Stoa means porch. Zeno taught there, free to anyone passing, so his students were called Stoics: the porch people.

steps.line: Today: the job that ended, a box of desk things, a bookshop window. Not every loss leads somewhere good. But a few pages can still change a life.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Your friend just lost their job. Going by the Stoics, what’s the wise thing to say today?
o: “That’s awful. I’m here. What do you need?”
“Think of it as a good voyage!”
steps.why: Zeno called his wreck a good voyage years later, looking back. Epictetus said that when a friend grieves, you should sympathize, even groan with him. Kindness now; meaning can come later.

say: here’s what i love. the stoics never said the wreck was good. losing everything hurts, and nobody should tell a grieving person it happened for a reason.

zeno went on to teach that money, cargo and good luck are not what makes a life good. only a good character is. the sea took his fortune. it couldn’t touch that. and the school he started still has students today.

steps.q: Another old version has Zeno say: “You do well, Fortune, driving me to philosophy.” What does that line show?
o: He blamed bad luck for his ruin
Loss pushed him toward what mattered
He thanked Fortune for his cargo
steps.why: He doesn’t pretend the wreck was nothing. He sees where it pushed him: away from cargo, toward wisdom.

today.say: zeno’s new life began with a few pages read aloud in a shop. the stoics kept that habit: read a little every day, and carry one line with you. today, read one page of something wise, and keep one line.
options: then open it today. one page is enough.
